![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186133900/plots/05e4b4ae17d397f993aa28e75c5116af7cde15e16f844f62a5febc57a4c8518a.png)

Given $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 2 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}$, calculate $\oint_{\partial D}P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy$ over the positively oriented annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial D}P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_D - 2 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):2\le r\le 5,0\le\theta\le2\pi\}.$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D - 2 x^{2} - 2 y^{2}\,\mathrm dA & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}-2\left(((r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2)\cdot r\right)\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}-2\left(r^{2}(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\cdot r\right)\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}- 2 r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\,\mathrm d \theta\cdot \int_{2}^{5}- 2 r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot \int_{2}^{5}r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot \frac{r^{4}}{4}\big|_{2}^{5}\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot (\left(\frac{625}{4}\right)-\left(4\right))\\ & =-2\cdot\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\cdot \left((5)^{4}-\left((2)^{4}\right)\right)\\ & =- \pi\cdot \left(625-\left(16\right)\right)\\ & =- 609 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

Calculate $\oint_{\partial D}(2 x^{4} y + \frac{2 x^{2} y^{3}}{3})\,\mathrm dx+(- \frac{2 x^{3} y^{2}}{3} - 2 x y^{4})\,\mathrm dy$, where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=2 x^{4} y + \frac{2 x^{2} y^{3}}{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=- \frac{2 x^{3} y^{2}}{3} - 2 x y^{4}.$ So,

For $\partial P/\partial y$ we hold $x$ fixed, and for $\partial Q/\partial x$ we hold $y$ fixed. The component derivatives, including zero contributions, are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(2 x^{4} y + \frac{2 x^{2} y^{3}}{3}\right)=\left(2 x^{4}\right)+\left(2 x^{2} y^{2}\right)=2 x^{4} + 2 x^{2} y^{2}\\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- \frac{2 x^{3} y^{2}}{3} - 2 x y^{4}\right)=\left(- 2 y^{4}\right)+\left(- 2 x^{2} y^{2}\right)=- 2 x^{2} y^{2} - 2 y^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=2 x^{4} + 2 x^{2} y^{2},\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=- 2 x^{2} y^{2} - 2 y^{4}.$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial D}(2 x^{4} y + \frac{2 x^{2} y^{3}}{3})\,\mathrm dx+(- \frac{2 x^{3} y^{2}}{3} - 2 x y^{4})\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D\left(- 2 x^{2} y^{2} - 2 y^{4}-(2 x^{4} + 2 x^{2} y^{2})\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D(- 2 x^{4} - 4 x^{2} y^{2} - 2 y^{4})\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D - 2 \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)^{2}\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):2\le r\le 5,0\le\theta\le2\pi\}.$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D - 2 \left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right)^{2}\,\mathrm dA & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}-2\left(((r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2)^2\cdot r\right)\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}-2\left(r^{4}(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)^2\cdot r\right)\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}- 2 r^{5}\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\,\mathrm d \theta\cdot \int_{2}^{5}- 2 r^{5}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot \int_{2}^{5}r^{5}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot \frac{r^{6}}{6}\big|_{2}^{5}\\ & =- 4 \pi\cdot (\left(\frac{15625}{6}\right)-\left(\frac{32}{3}\right))\\ & =-2\cdot\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cdot \left((5)^{6}-\left((2)^{6}\right)\right)\\ & =- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\cdot \left(15625-\left(64\right)\right)\\ & =- 10374 \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186133900/plots/85391332ef9a234e4da186f45122f8dd922b7fb19f05c3f5796aed07d1627b61.png)

Let $\partial R$ be the boundary of the region $R,$ shown above. Use Green's theorem to calculate the following integral:

$\oint_{\partial R}\mathbf F\cdot\mathrm d\mathbf r=\oint_{\partial R}(- 3 x y^{2})\,\mathrm dx+(y^{3})\,\mathrm dy=$

{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=- 3 x y^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=y^{3}.$ So,

For $\partial P/\partial y$ we hold $x$ fixed, and for $\partial Q/\partial x$ we hold $y$ fixed. The component derivatives, including zero contributions, are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- 3 x y^{2}\right)=\left(- 6 x y\right)=- 6 x y\\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(y^{3}\right)=\left(0\right)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 6 x y,\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=0.$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial R}(- 3 x y^{2})\,\mathrm dx+(y^{3})\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_R\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_R\left(0-(- 6 x y)\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_R 6 x y\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

As we saw earlier, we can use Green's theorem to write our line integral in polar coordinates as 

$$\oint_{\partial R}(- 3 x y^{2})\,\mathrm dx+(y^{3})\,\mathrm dy=\iint_\Delta 3r^3\sin(2\theta)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta.$$

But this time, our region $R$ (in polar coordinates) is given by 

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):2\le r\le 3,0\le\theta<2\pi\}.$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_\Delta 3r^3\sin(2\theta)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm d\theta & =3\cdot \int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{3}r^3\sin(2\theta)\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =3\cdot \int_{0}^{2 \pi}\sin(2\theta)\,\mathrm d \theta\cdot \int_{2}^{3}r^3\,\mathrm d r\\ & =3\cdot \frac{\cos(2\theta)}{-2}\big|_{0}^{2 \pi}\cdot \frac{r^4}{4}\big|_{2}^{3}\\ & =3\cdot (\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right))\cdot (\left(\frac{81}{4}\right)-\left(4\right))\\ & =-1\cdot\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\cdot (1-1)\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot \left((3)^{4}-\left((2)^{4}\right)\right)\\ & =- \frac{3}{2}\cdot (1-1)\cdot\frac{1}{4}\cdot \left(81-\left(16\right)\right)\\ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $\oint_{\partial D}(- 3 x^{3} - 3 x y^{2})\,\mathrm dx+(- 6 x^{2} y + 3 y^{3})\,\mathrm dy$, where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=- 3 x^{3} - 3 x y^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=- 6 x^{2} y + 3 y^{3}.$ Therefore,

For $\partial P/\partial y$ we hold $x$ fixed, and for $\partial Q/\partial x$ we hold $y$ fixed. The component derivatives, including zero contributions, are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- 3 x^{3} - 3 x y^{2}\right)=\left(0\right)+\left(- 6 x y\right)=- 6 x y\\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- 6 x^{2} y + 3 y^{3}\right)=\left(0\right)+\left(- 12 x y\right)=- 12 x y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 6 x y,\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=- 12 x y.$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial D}(- 3 x^{3} - 3 x y^{2})\,\mathrm dx+(- 6 x^{2} y + 3 y^{3})\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D\left(- 12 x y-(- 6 x y)\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D - 6 x y\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as $\Delta_1\setminus\Delta_2,$ where

- $\Delta_1=\{(x,y):-3\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 3\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- $\Delta_2=\{(x,y):-2\le x\le 0,1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D - 6 x y\,\mathrm dA & =\iint_{\Delta_1}- 6 x y\,\mathrm dA-\iint_{\Delta_2}- 6 x y\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\int_{0}^{3}\int_{-3}^{1}- 6 x y\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y-\int_{1}^{2}\int_{-2}^{0}- 6 x y\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\\ & =\int_{-3}^{1}- 6 x\,\mathrm d x\cdot \int_{0}^{3}y\,\mathrm d y-\int_{-2}^{0}- 6 x\,\mathrm d x\cdot \int_{1}^{2}y\,\mathrm d y\\ & =- 3 x^{2}\big|_{-3}^{1}\cdot \frac{y^2}{2}\big|_{0}^{3}-\left(- 3 x^{2}\big|_{-2}^{0}\cdot \frac{y^2}{2}\big|_{1}^{2}\right)\\ & =(\left(-3\right)-\left(-27\right))\cdot (\left(\frac{9}{2}\right)-\left(0\right))-(\left(0\right)-\left(-12\right))\cdot (\left(2\right)-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right))\\ & =\left(24\right)\cdot \left(\frac{9}{2}\right)-\left(12\right)\cdot \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\\ & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $\oint_{\partial D}(- 2 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x)\,\mathrm dx+(- 2 x^{4} y^{2} + 2 y)\,\mathrm dy$, where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=- 2 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x$ and $Q(x,y)=- 2 x^{4} y^{2} + 2 y.$ Therefore,

For $\partial P/\partial y$ we hold $x$ fixed, and for $\partial Q/\partial x$ we hold $y$ fixed. The component derivatives, including zero contributions, are

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(- 2 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x\right)=\left(0\right)+\left(- 6 x^{3} y^{2}\right)=- 6 x^{3} y^{2}\\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} & =\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(- 2 x^{4} y^{2} + 2 y\right)=\left(0\right)+\left(- 8 x^{3} y^{2}\right)=- 8 x^{3} y^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=- 6 x^{3} y^{2},\qquad\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=- 8 x^{3} y^{2}.$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial D}(- 2 x^{3} y^{3} - 2 x)\,\mathrm dx+(- 2 x^{4} y^{2} + 2 y)\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D\left(- 8 x^{3} y^{2}-(- 6 x^{3} y^{2})\right)\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\iint_D - 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as $\Delta_1\setminus\Delta_2,$ where

- $\Delta_1=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,-2\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- $\Delta_2=\{(x,y):1\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 0\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D - 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm dA & =\iint_{\Delta_1}- 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm dA-\iint_{\Delta_2}- 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm dA\\ & =\int_{-2}^{1}\int_{-1}^{3}- 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y-\int_{-1}^{0}\int_{1}^{2}- 2 x^{3} y^{2}\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\\ & =\int_{-1}^{3}- 2 x^{3}\,\mathrm d x\cdot \int_{-2}^{1}y^{2}\,\mathrm d y-\int_{1}^{2}- 2 x^{3}\,\mathrm d x\cdot \int_{-1}^{0}y^{2}\,\mathrm d y\\ & =\frac{-2x^4}{4}\big|_{-1}^{3}\cdot \frac{y^3}{3}\big|_{-2}^{1}-\frac{-2x^4}{4}\big|_{1}^{2}\cdot \frac{y^3}{3}\big|_{-1}^{0}\\ & =(\left(- \frac{81}{2}\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right))\cdot (\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)-\left(- \frac{8}{3}\right))-(\left(-8\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right))\cdot (\left(0\right)-\left(- \frac{1}{3}\right))\\ & =\left(-40\right)\cdot \left(3\right)-\left(- \frac{15}{2}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\\ & =- \frac{235}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
